SUMMARY

The Master Plan for DNGIR, 2041 aims to create a modern industrial development hub of
global standards. The plan envisages the development of globally competitive industrial
investment areas, and a modern education hub. It intends to make the town act as an
incubator for innovation and startups for the development of new technologies. The
proposed industries include IT and ITeS, electronics and electrical (semi-conductor chips,
etc.), automobile industry, solar panel manufacturing, food processing industry, textile
and garment industry, defense equipment manufacturing industry, cement and tiles
industry, and film industry. The upcoming Western Delhi Freight Corridor (DFC) from
Dadri to Mumbai and the Eastern Peripheral Expressway will help in promoting and
developing world class logistics infrastructure to support planned industries.

The planning area has high regional accessibility through road, rail, and upcoming airport
at Jewar. Further, with the neighboring existing industrial townships of Noida, Greater
Noida and Yamuna Expressway, this development will become one of the key industrial
regions for IT and ITES along with other cutting-edge industries. The Master Plan for
DNGIR, 2041 also intends to attract global manufacturing companies through provision
of various categories of large plots.

High accessibility is promoted within the town as nearly 14 percent of the land in the
planning area is reserved for transport infrastructure. Attempts have been made to
ensure equitable, effective, and efficient connectivity through grid-iron pattern
development.

To strike a balance between sustainable development and economic buoyancy,
substantial provision of green spaces is made. Nearly 18 percent of land in the planning
area is allocated to green spaces. Inclusive planning and sustainable development are
governing feature of the Master Plan for DNGIR, 2041.

Conservation of large water bodies of the size of one hectare and more and reduced
dependency on fresh water sources by recycling and reuse of wastewater are some of the
other important features of water sensitive planning being proposed in this Plan. The
Plan encourages use and reuse of water with reduced reliance on freshwater resources.
Physical and social infrastructure shall act as the backbone of the DNGIR. The Plan
intends to develop smart physical infrastructure such as smart utility ducts, smart waste
management sites and provision of smart energy with low carbon footprint.

High rise, medium density, group housing based residential development is proposed in
the Master Plan. The Plan also proposes safe and secure neighborhoods with availability
of basic amenities within walking distance in each sector. The plan intends to provide
housing for industrial labor as well.

1. INTRODUCTION

1.1 INTRODUCTION

The Master Plan for Dadri-Noida-Ghaziabad Investment Region (DNGIR), 2041 is being
prepared under the UP Industrial Development Area Act 1976, under clause 6 which
allows an Authority to prepare a master plan for a notified area. The key function of a
master plan is to promote planned development within its regional setting, which link the
new town to surrounding developed areas.

The notified DNGIR area has been identified as one of the seven proposed investment
regions in the first phase of the Delhi Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC), which will be
implemented in phases with the development of supporting infrastructure and early bird
projects. The DNGIR is a part of the Western Dedicated Freight Corridor (WDFC), which
serves as a critical transport link running along the Delhi Mumbai Industrial Corridor’s
(DMIC) entire length. This area has excellent connectivity through road and rail links to
Uttar Pradesh and rest of India. It includes Noida; Ghaziabad, the hub of engineering and
electronics industries; Greater Noida; and another newly planned city Yamuna
Expressway Industrial Area, which houses the Jewar Airport in the vicinity. These
adjoining urban areas have a well-evolved road network, state of the art physical and
social infrastructure along with some of the best residential, commercial, institutional
and entertainment areas.

The new town of DNGIR has the notified planning area of 209.11 square kilometers and
comprises of 84 villages located in the districts of Gautam Buddha Nagar and
Bulandshahr. In the DNGIR planning area, out of a total of 84 villages, 63 villages are in
Bulandshahr district and 21 villages in Gautam Buddha Nagar. Sikandrabad town is
located outside the DNGIR planning area in Bulandshahr district of Uttar Pradesh state.
Parts of two industrial areas – Sikandrabad Industrial Area I and Sikandrabad Industrial
Area II – are also located in the notified area of the DNGIR.

The topography of the DNGIR planning area is plain and some uneven lands can be also
found. 63 villages of Bulandshahr district located between 28˚4’ and 28˚ north latitudes
and 77˚ and 78˚ east longitudes form a part of the DNGIR planning area. The part of DNGIR
planning area in Bulandshahr district is situated in the Upper Doab of the Ganga and
Yamuna rivers, which forms its eastern and western boundaries respectively, and
separates it from district Moradabad and Budaun in the east. It is also bound by the
district Ghaziabad in the north and district Aligarh in the south. Remaining 21 villages of
Gautam Buddha Nagar district form another significant part of the DNGIR planning area.
This part is situated between the parallels of 28˚ 6' to 28˚ 40' north latitude and 77˚ 17' -
77˚ 42' east longitude.

Some of the critical infrastructure is already in place to propel industrial growth in the
DNGIR. For example, sustained supply of electricity could be ensured through a 3,500
MW gas-based electricity power plant built near Dadri, a settlement located near the
DNGIR. To ensure sustained supply of water, the Ganga Canal passes along the DNGIR
planning area. The DNGIR is one of the key nodes of the Delhi Mumbai Freight Corridor
(DMIC) because of its proximity to the terminal point of the Western Dedicated Freight
Corridor.

   1

The approximate distance between DNGIR and Ghaziabad through NH 91 GT Road is 24
km. The distance between the DNGIR and Noida through Bulandshahr Road is 33 km.
Similarly, the distance between the DNGIR to Jewar town through Bulandshahr-Jewar
road is 32 km. The towns of Dadri, Khurja and Sikandrabad are near the DNGIR within
about 5 km from the boundary of the DNGIR and connected through NH-91 GT Road.

The notified DNGIR planning area has been experiencing rapid population growth since
2001 mainly because of natural increase and settling of families living in villages around
Dadri town. Rapid growth of population has also occurred due to the emergence of two
new towns i.e., Noida and Greater Noida. Since 1981, Dadri has also witnessed high
population growth rate due to the generation of economic opportunities and its location
along the National Highway 91. Employment opportunities, strategic location and
infrastructure development are other major causes for this pattern of growth.

Many developments have been proposed and are taking place around the proposed
DNGIR planning area. Some of the important projects identified around the DNGIR are
Integrated Industrial Township at Greater Noida, Multi Modal Transport Hub (MMTH) at
Boraki and Multimodal Logistics Hub (MMLH) at Greater Noida.

Land is the most significant element of any form of city planning. So far, land acquisition
has remained one of the favorite modes of land procurement for building new towns in
this area. However, currently land assembly has become a relatively popular means of
procuring land for development to build new towns whereby government authorities or
private entities directly negotiate with owners to procure land. In the same vein, the
DNGIR is also expected to be developed by largely assembling land from 84 villages.
However, some land acquisition is unavoidable.

Overall, the DNGIR is strategically located with the very high potential to become a
growing industrial hub in the vicinity of Greater Noida. Ample supply of water through
the Ganga Canal, uninterrupted power supply from Dadri power plant, and excellent road,
rail and most importantly upcoming global air connectivity through Jewar Airport make
the DNGIR a hugely advantageous location for modern industrial development.

Based on the brief contextual discussion above, the vision and objectives of the Master
Plan for DNGIR, 2041 has been discussed below.

1.2 VISION AND OBJECTIVES OF THE MASTER PLAN FOR DNGIR, 2041

Master Plan for the DNGIR 2041 envisions to promote economic buoyancy through
industrial development, and sustainability through inclusive planning and enhanced use
of renewable sources of energy. The objectives to achieve the vision are as follows:

 •   To develop the planning area as a globally competitive industrial investment hub of
   northern India.

 •   To prepare the plan focused on economic buoyancy as well as sustainable
   development.

 •   To spatially integrate abadi areas with planned new town developments.

   2

1.3 GUIDING PRINCIPLES OF THE MASTER PLAN FOR DNGIR, 2041

To achieve its objectives, the following guiding principles shall be adopted:

1.3.1 Robust, Compact and Flexible Structure for Future Development

New town development should be able to adapt to new situations whether political,
economic, and social. The DNGIR development is proposed in five phases, which will
allow for flexibility in the development process.

1.3.2 Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle of Water

Water is a scarce resource in the investment region. The plan proposes that available
freshwater sources should be used in an efficient manner. Only water efficient industries
should be allowed in the area and rainwater harvesting shall be proactively promoted. As
far as possible, demand for potable water and industrial use should be minimized by
recycling and reuse. Adequate physical infrastructure is proposed to ensure effective
treatment of wastewater in the new town.

1.3.3 Creating a Knowledge based Society

Increasingly knowledge and innovation are seen as the key drivers of a progressive urban
settlement. Knowledge City is proposed in the planning area where Education, Medical-
Hub and High-Tech industries and modern infrastructure will play a critical role.

1.3.4 Use of Renewable Energy

Use of renewable energy should be encouraged to contribute to a clean, healthy, and
sustainable environment. This is also in line with the energy policy of Government of
India and country’s global commitments. Public buildings should use solar energy to
reduce the load on the National Grid. The plan proposes the provision of piped cooking
gas to promote extensive use of natural gas.

1.3.5 Create a Sustainable New Town

Sustainability is an overarching guiding principle of development in the DNGIR and a set
of policies will be implemented in all aspects, such as ecological, social, cultural, and
economic, to facilitate sustainable development of the new town.

1.3.6 Minimize Negative Social Impacts

Master Plan for DNGIR 2041 proposes ‘no relocation policy’ of the existing population
living in villages. Instead of displacement of rural population, abadi areas are proposed
to be densified to create possibilities for incorporation of future population in the existing
rural settlements. Job creation for the farmers is also proposed through a particular focus
on the development of food production industry in the new town.

   3

1.3.7 Maximum Connectivity, Circulation and Accessibility

The Plan for DNGIR, 2041, further proposes an effective public transport system to make
available excellent internal accessibility by clear and functional road structure.

1.3.8 Waste Management

An existing or new town would surely generate waste of different kinds. To mitigate
major environmental impacts, Master Plan for DNGIR, 2041 proposes to reduce urban
and industrial wastes. A unique waste management system is envisaged with a proposal
for the development of an integrated solid waste management facility.

To actualize the above-mentioned objectives and sustainable goals, the Master Plan for
DNGIR, 2041 proposes several development strategies to:

 •   Develop it as a global manufacturing and trading hub and as an engine of economic
   growth.
 •   Act as an incubator for innovation and startups for the development of new
   technologies.
 •   House state of the art education hub as well as develop world class logistics
   infrastructure to support industry and workforce.
 •   Develop smart infrastructure such as smart waste management and smart energy
   production facilities.
 •   Conserve large water bodies to reduce dependency on fresh water sources by
   recycling and reusing wastewater.
 •   Promote sustainable a model of development with low carbon footprint.

1.4   Methodology for Plan Development

Keeping in view the democratic procedures and based on the statutory requirements,
inclusive and collaborative methodology has been followed for the preparation of the
Master Plan for the DNGIR, 2041. This included reconnaissance surveys, multiple field
visits, finalization and verification of planning area, and consultation workshops with
village pradhans, sarpanches, industrialists, and other important stakeholders, etc.
Several presentations were also made before stakeholders before finalization of the
planning proposals.

The existing policies for industrial development in Uttar Pradesh and the central
government were examined, and major provisions of these policies have been
incorporated in strategies for time bound development and action plans.

1.5   CONCLUSION

Master Plan for DNGIR 2041 is intended to plan sustainable and economically developed
industrial new town. The new town is planned to be developed as a major investment
hub due to the strategic spatial location and connectivity with the surrounding areas
making it accessible for building international trade and commerce. The new town is
expected to become a strategically important hub of industrial development with many
spin-off effects.

2. DEMOGRAPHIC CHARACTERISTICS

2.1 INTRODUCTION

The DNGIR planning area is comprised of 84 villages with 209.11 sq km area and
population of 1,51,778 as per Census of India 2011. Population projections of the DNGIR
are made based on all possible and pragmatic factors. However, the results may differ as
per the changing scenario over time.

2.2 EXISTING DEMOGRAPHIC PROFILE

2.2.1 Distribution Of Population

According to the Census of India, 1991, before the formation of the Gautam Buddha Nagar
district, total population of the 84 villages located in the notified Dadri-Noida-Ghaziabad-
Investment-Region was 1,10,904. The 2001 census revealed that total population
residing in the 84 notified villages increased to 1,29,638, growing at a decadal growth
rate of 17 percent during 1991-2001. This decadal growth rate of 84 villages is slower
when compared to decadal rural growth rate at national and state, which is 18 percent,
17 percent respectively. This growth rate is, however, greater than the district at 16
percent. Population in the notified villages increased to 1,51,778 in 2011 as per the
census, growing at the rate of nearly 18 per cent during 2001-2011 (see Table 2.1).

2.2.2 Age Composition

As per Census of India 2011, children up to 15 years of age constituted 38.74 per cent of
the total population, whereas working age group of 16-60 years accounted for 55.05 per
cent. Within this age group, a relatively younger set of people between the ages of 15 and
40 years constituted as much as 40.79 per cent. Only 6.20 per cent of the population
consisted of citizens above the age of 60.

2.2.3 Sex Ratio

Sex ratio of population in the notified area was 889 as per Census 2011, which is on the
lower side as compared to sex ratio of 995 in rural areas of Uttar Pradesh.

   5

2.2.4 Literacy Rate

The average literacy rate of the notified area as per the 2011 census is 59.94 per cent.
There are 4 villages in the investment region, which have a literacy rate of less than 40
per cent, which is extremely low. As per the Census 2011, the male literacy rate was 72.13
per cent and female literacy rate is only 50.33 per cent in 2011.

2.2.5 Household Size

As per Census of India 2011, the average household size in villages in the DNGIR is 6
persons. Data further reveals that nearly 30.5 per cent of the households have a
household size of 4 to 5 persons. Of the remaining about 54.3 per cent of households have
more than 6 persons per household and 16.9 per cent have less than 4 persons per
household.

The existing population growth trends are beneficial for projecting population for the
plan period up to 2041.

2.3 POPULATION PROJECTIONS

Population growth of the area is expected to be higher in comparison to new towns
located away from large metropolitan towns. For calculating the natural growth within
the abadi areas three methods i.e., arithmetic method, incremental method, and
geometric progression are used for projecting population and the average decadal
growth. Amongst all three methods, the highest increase in population is observed
through incremental method and the lowest by arithmetic increase method.

With an average growth rate, the total population of abadi areas in the DNGIR is projected
as 2,47,693 persons in 2041. Adopting the middle path, an average decadal population
growth rate of 18 percent is assumed, which roughly equals the national urban average
population growth rate.

To calculate the total population of the DNGIR, it is assumed that the gross town density
for 2041 shall be approximately 30 persons per hectare (pph). Based on the town density
assumption, total population of the DNGIR is estimated to be 6,33,000, which is to be
accommodated within the DNGIR. This means 3,79,800 people need to be accommodated
in the DNGIR and in the surrounding towns (see Table 2.2).

It is further assumed that the workforce participation rate would be 40 percent of the
total population, which comes out to be 2,53,200 persons.

3. ECONOMY

3.1 INTRODUCTION

The economy is the backbone of a town to provide the financial basis for its physical
growth and wellbeing for the inhabitants.

The Master Plan for the DNGIR, 2041 focuses on the town's robust economy with the goal
of developing the new town as an industrial center for Uttar Pradesh. The unique
positioning of the township would play a critical role in establishing the town as a
national and worldwide destination for investors seeking to grow exponentially. This
chapter focuses on the workforce including workers participation rate, sectoral
distribution of workers, and the nature of future occupational structure.

3.2 EXISTING OCCUPATIONAL STRUCTURE

3.2.1 Workers Participation Rate

The major source of livelihood within the DNGIR is predominantly agriculture. Out of the
total population, only 33 per cent of the population is classified as workers and 67 percent
of the population falls in the category of non-workers. Significantly, out of the total
workers, 74 per cent are the main workers and 26 per cent are marginal workers.

Only one village has more than 80 per cent working population due to easy accessibility
to Eastern Periphery Expressway and NH-91, which provides economic opportunities in
the vicinity. 10 villages have 40 per cent to 60 per cent worker population and 70 villages
have 20 per cent to 40 per cent. Another 2 villages have less than 20 per cent of the
worker population, and Raghunathpur village is un-inhabited.

3.2.2 Sectoral Distribution of Workers

Amongst the main workers, 48 per cent of workers are engaged in the primary sector as
agriculture laborers. The master plan recommends several strategies for the main,
marginal, and non-workers in the planning area.

3.3 FUTURE OCCUPATIONAL STRUCTURE

Primary source of livelihoods of the existing population in the DNGIR is agriculture and
related activities with some industrial sector employment in surrounding areas.

The planning area being a greenfield township, 40 percent workforce participation rate
is being assumed, resulting in a total estimated workforce of 2,53,200 by 2041. The
remaining 60 percent is considered dependent population. Moreover, out of the total
workforce, 65 percent of these workers would be working in industrial sectors and the
rest 35 percent of workers would be engaged in non-industrial sectors such as the service
sector (see Table 3.1).

4.1 INTRODUCTION

Trade and commerce are defined as fundamental economic activities. The area has some
commercial activity like dairy, poultry, fish, and agro-based trading of products.

(a) Principles of Water Management

Master Plan for the DNGIR 2041 has adopted a holistic approach to water management,
which has three parts:

 •   Capture rain
 •   Collect and treat used water and
 •   Recycle water

Economic development within the watershed must take place in harmony with the
physical environment.

(b) Water Demand

Water demand for the DNGIR is estimated at 300 MLD by 2041 including distribution and
transmission losses for a total population of 6,33,000. Within this, industrial water
requirement is estimated to be 212 MLD for an area of 84.21 sq km. The domestic water
requirement is estimated to be 135 LPCD whereas that of industrial area the demand is
25 kiloliter per day per hectare as per CPHEEO norms.

For sustainable ground water development, withdrawal of ground water shall be zero.
Upper Ganga Canal and its branches have been identified as the main source of water
intake. Broad provisions for the intake of water and its supply include:

 •   Master Plan proposes to pump water from Upper Ganga Canal and its branches.
 •   Water would be stored intermittently in reservoirs, which shall be designed based
   on detailed engineering studies and investigations while formulating detailed
   project reports.
 •   Water stored in reservoirs shall be used to supply throughout the year.

(c) Water Distribution System

An efficient water supply system for transmission from canal water to individual
households is proposed. The laying of the water supply network shall be executed as per
phasing. These are water intake, water treatment plants, clear water reservoirs,
distribution centers and distribution network.

(d) Water Treatment

Water quality requirements of various types of users will be different due to difference
in their nature of activities. Type of water treatment process to be adopted will depend
on the raw water quality. Water received from the Upper Ganga Canal and its branches
shall be tested to determine the quality and treatment methods. Type of water treatment
process to be adopted will entirely depend on the raw water quality.

8.5 FACILITIES FOR MODAL INTERCHANGE

Delhi Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC) is a global manufacturing and industrial
corridor along with planned Dedicated Freight Corridor (DFC) by Government of India’s
National Infrastructure Corridor Development Corporation (NICDC). The DFC comprising
of two distinct corridors namely Western Dedicated Freight Corridor (WDFC) and
Eastern Dedicated Freight Corridor (EDFC) have been conceived as high capacity, high
speed, freight rail line by the Ministry of Railways. The proposed DFC alignment is
envisaged to be supplemented by significant infrastructure facilities proposed as a part
of the DMIC, which together will enhance economic development of the DMIC region. The
proposed investment regions (IR) under NICDC i.e., DNGIR is proposed to be self-
contained industrial township with world-class infrastructure, road, and rail connectivity
for freight movement to and from ports and logistics hubs.

The proposed investment region in Uttar Pradesh Sub-region has been conceived as a
model industrial corridor of international standards with an emphasis on developing it
as a global manufacturing and trading hub.

The locational advantage of the DNGIR is considered important having its high
connectivity by Delhi-Howrah Railway Line and the proposed DFC corridor as an
integrated Multi Modal Logistics Hub (MMLH) along with Multi Modal Logistics Park
(MMLP).

8.5.1 Multi Modal Logistics Park (MMLP)

The proposed MMLP for bulk cargo shall function as inter-modal freight handling facility
with mechanized material handling provisions containing warehouses, specialized cold
chain facilities, freight container terminals and bulk cargo terminals. The services such as
customs clearance, provision of processing activities such as sorting or grading,
aggregation, disaggregation, cold storage, etc. shall serve as a major cargo consolidation
and distribution hubs. The major functions of the MMLP will be:

 •   To act as hubs for freight movement enabling freight aggregation and distribution.
 •   To provide connectivity with road, rail, and other modes of transport in order to
   promote multi-modal freight transportation.
 •   To provide modern mechanized warehousing spaces to satisfy requirements of
   different commodity groups.

8.5.2 Multimodal Transport Hub (MMTH)

A MMTH having facilities such as inter – city bus terminal, rail terminal, intra – city bus
and para transit terminals, multi – level parking facilities, commercial and public semi –
public uses and a business centre equipped with offices and business hotel
accommodation is proposed in the western region at the confluence of Delhi Kolkata
railway line with proposed 105m ROW Road, which is located near the vicinity of the
DNGIR.

8.6 ORBITAL RAIL CORRIDOR

According to the functional Transport Plan of NCRPB, 2031, an orbital rail corridor is
proposed to enhance regional connectivity along the Eastern Peripheral Expressway. The

11.   PHASING OF DEVELOPMENT

11.1 INTRODUCTION

The phasing of development is a key to the success of the DNGIR as it guides the processes
of land procurement, availability of funds, sequence of development activities in the
DNGIR and more importantly, the setting up of industries. Development of the DNGIR
shall be carried out in five phases.

11.2 LAND ASSEMBLY MODELS

For the town to be developed as envisaged and Master Plan to be successfully
implemented by keeping in view timeline for industrial growth and physical development
of the planning area is divided into five phases. The first phase shall involve the land
purchase and the subsequent infrastructure development (arterial and sub-arterial
roads) by the Noida Authority itself. The remaining 4 phases shall be developed
subsequently and to be extended till 2047 to ease out the acquisition and development
process. For Phases II, III, IV and IV, land can be assembled through land acquisition or
direct land purchase, land pooling or land aggregation and licensing. Flexibility is ensured
to develop the sectors in the master plan by these methods. These methods have been
further discussed below.

11.2.1 Land Acquisition or Direct Land Purchase

Land can be acquired for development purpose as per Uttar Pradesh Land Acquisition
Policy 2011. In lieu of that landowners should be given adequate compensation and other
facilities, their interest be protected and they get the adequate benefits of development
as per the policy. Other than this, direct land purchase through negotiations is a process
whereby land is procured from farmers or landowners after a mutual agreement about
land values which benefit both parties. Land is then developed in accordance with master
plan provisions and planning norms for various uses and activities.

11.2.2 Land Pooling

This policy allows industrial development authorities to execute expressions of interest
with farmers and invite applications from those who wish to sell their lands to the
government. The Uttar Pradesh Land Pooling Policy, 2017 is applicable where more than
80 percent landowners are willing to participate in a land pooling scheme for
development. As per the policy, farmer will get compensation for 75 percent of the
acquired land and additionally get back the remaining 25 percent compensation in the
form of a plot of land after the authority develops basic infrastructure in the area.

11.2.3 Land Aggregation and Licensing

As per Uttar Pradesh Industrial Investment and Employment Promotion Policy 2022, for
facilitating land aggregation for private industrial parks, the government will provide
assistance in order to help private parties acquire land outside of Industrial Development
Authorities, Housing Development Authorities, Urban Local Bodies, or other designated
locations. It is applicable to Private Industrial Parks with at least 5 units and more than
100 acres, as long as no one unit takes up more than 80% of the allotted industrial space.

   67

A license will be given in support of this upon the purchase of 25% of the total intended
land area (with a registered sale deed). No one else in such licensed areas may approve a
map, and development and construction are to be regulated. In the permitted area, the
developer will have the sole right to develop or build. Within 18 months, a Detailed
Project Report (DPR) must be submitted. By then, 60% of the entire land acquisition
project (including the land pooling agreement) must be finished. Map approval must
occur after 75% of the land has been acquired (including the land pooling agreement)
and within two years of the license's issuance. The organization that approves maps is
UPSIDA. If there are any difficulties in acquiring the remaining land after the developer
has gathered 80% of the total proposed land, UPSIDA will purchase it upon production of
a bank guarantee for the comparable sum.

12.4 ZONING REGULATIONS

The Zoning regulations identify land uses such as residential, commercial, industrial,
institutional, public, and semi-public facilities, transportation, parks, open spaces, and
other specific land uses. The zoning regulations are also required for the ancillary or
incidental activities that are not shown separately on the land use map. To ensure public
health, welfare, and security of the public, provisions of ancillary or incidental activities
or utilities are required to be made by competent authority in accordance with the zoning
regulations and the specific requirements of a particular scheme.

12.5 PERMISSIBLE AND PERMITTED USES IN VARIOUS LAND USE ZONES

One of the goals of the Master Plan is to create balanced and livable city with a coherent
social life. Public should be able to live a healthy lifestyle, get access to work through
public transport system, and it should be a child friendly city The foundation of the
development will be based on equity, justice, and legal certainty. The Master Plan
specifies various land uses in conformity with use premises and other critical issues. The
different activities or utilities to be provided or planned in the proposed main land use
categories are as under:

 •   Permitted Uses: These activities or utilities are ancillary to the main land use and
   are planned and permitted.

 •   Conditional Permissible Uses: These activities will be planned or allowed under
   specific conditions keeping in view the infrastructure and its environmental impact
   on the surrounding areas.

 •   With Special permission of Board: These activities can be permitted if the Board
   of the Authority permits.

 •   Not Permitted: These activities shall not be permitted in the particular land use.

The urban form should allow for development flexibility while also providing
opportunities for easy development of public infrastructure and facilities like
transportation space, physical and social infrastructure, green space, urban forest, and
water bodies.

12.8 MANDATORY PROVISIONS

12.8.1 Rooftop Solar Power Panels

Solar power plants on the building rooftops that cover 50 percent of the clear rooftop
area are required for all structures (commercial, institutional, and industrial buildings)
with more than 10,000 sq m of built-up area as well as residential structures including
group housing with 100 dwelling units or more and integrated townships with 10
hectares or more area. Guidelines on Off-Grid and Decentralized Solar Applications and
Rooftop and Other Small Solar Power Plants set by the Ministry of Renewable Energy,
Government of India, must be adhered to while installing solar power plants on building
rooftops.

The buildings implementing this provision shall be granted additional 10 percent FAR
over and above the prescribed FAR for land use typology. Building plans that are
submitted for the competent authority's approval by the applicant must explicitly
disclose information on rooftop solar power plants, based on which the competent
authority shall provide additional FAR. When granting the building completion
certification, the competent authority shall make the completion and operation of the
rooftop solar power plant a necessary requirement.

12.8.2 Rainwater Harvesting

Rooftop rainwater harvesting systems are required to be developed and installed in every
building, regardless of use type or size. In general, the amount of rooftop water that can
be collected should be considered while designing a rainwater harvesting system. The
Central Ground Water Board has provided the following calculation to measure how
much water should be collected from rooftops:

Total quantity of water to be collected (cu m) = Roof Top Area (sq m) x Average Monsoon
Rainfall (m) x 0.8.

The Average rainfall for the DNGIR shall be considered as 620 mm.

14.1 STATE AND CENTRAL GOVERNMENT POLICIES

Since New Noida is part of the Western Dedicated Freight Corridor (WDFC) and serves as
a critical transport link running along the Delhi Mumbai Industrial Corridor’s (DMIC)
entire length, new industrial town would be of great importance nationally. The New
Noida has a huge potential due to excellent connectivity through road and rail to the rest
of the country. Relatively easily, the New Noida could be integrated with Noida and
Ghaziabad, the hub of engineering and electronics industries and Greater Noida, a
planned new city in the vicinity of the upcoming Jewar International Airport. Once
developed with modern road network, state of the art physical and social infrastructure
along with the creation of the best residential, commercial, institutional and
entertainment places, the New Noida would emerge as a nationally sought after
destination for industrial development.

Several existing state and national policies could potentially support the development of
the New Noida. Policies on land, industry, finance, housing and infrastructure are
analyzed in this chapter. More specifically advantages of land pooling procurement
policies relative to land acquisition are also examined. We shall also examine various
financial models adopted throughout the country to build new towns. Policy analysis is
conducted with the hope to select and use selected policy provisions when making
recommendations of the Master Plan of the New Noida, 2041.

14.1.1 Uttar Pradesh Land Pooling Policy, 2017

For urbanization, industrialization and infrastructure development land pooling as a
mode of land procurement has gained salience in India in the recent years. Due to the
voluntary participation of land owners in the development process, land pooling is a
sustainable option for land aggregation, as the land owners’ also have a share in
prosperity. The policy allows industrial authorities to execute expressions of interest
with farmers and invite applications from those who wish to sell their lands to the
government. The Uttar Pradesh Land Pooling Policy, 2017 is applicable where more than
80 percent land owners are willing to participate in a land pooling scheme for
development.

Unlike one-time settlement under the Land Acquisition Act, under the Uttar Pradesh Land
Pooling Policy, a farmer will get compensation for 75 percent of the acquired land and
additionally gets back the remaining 25 percent compensation in the form of a plot of
land after the authority develops basic infrastructure in the area. Until the developed plot
of land is given back to the owner, an annual rent of Rs. 60,000 per acre is given as
compensation. Of the 25 percent returned land, 80 percent land should be developed for
industrial use, 12 percent for residential and 8 percent for commercial use. A land owner
is also free to sell his whole share to anyone, including government. However, land
owners will also have to develop their lands as prescribed land use or sell land in 10 years
or else face penalties. At least 25 acres of land will be required for consideration under
the scheme and only continuous land parcels would be accepted.

   128

The administration would either acquire land using the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation
and Resettlement Act, 2013 or directly purchase it. Both would result in intense litigation
that could potentially stall any development project. So, this land pooling policy is
expected to facilitate the government to procure litigation-free land, and use land to
attract investment and further create a land bank.

14.1.2 Land Acquisition Policy, Uttar Pradesh, 2011

In order to implement infrastructure projects in the public sector including state
highways, canals, power projects, etc., the land acquisition process would be initiated by
following the Rules and Regulations as provided in the Land Acquisition Act 1894,
whereas the compensation of land would be fixed by mutual consent as per the provisions
of the Uttar Pradesh Land Acquisition (Determination of Compensation and Declaration
of Award by Agreement) Rules, 1997. Further all the benefits to those land owners whose
land is being acquired for these projects would be given under the Rehabilitation and
Resettlement Policy, 2010 (as amended) by the state government.

Local bodies such as undertakings like development authorities, industrial development
authorities, housing development boards, etc. acquire land for projects in order to
discharge their legal responsibility of planned development in which developed land is
allotted to public for their residential needs, to small units in service or industrial sector
and for community facilities. For such projects, the land will be acquired under the
provisions of Land Acquisition Act 1894. The following two options shall be available to
the land owners with a view to protecting their rights:

 •   Compensation shall be determined by the Governing Board of the public
   undertaking keeping liberal view and with mutual consent under the Settlement
   Rules, 1997. In addition to this, all the benefits available under Resettlement and
   Rehabilitation Policy shall also be available to all the affected farmers.

 •   Out of the total acquired land, 16 percent land after development shall be given back
   free of cost. Further, such land shall be transferable. Moreover, 50 percent of the
   developed land given to the land owner shall be developed for residential use and
   50 percent for non-residential uses like industrial, institutional, commercial or
   mixed use. The concerned body or undertaking or authority shall itself determine
   the relative percentage of non-residential use. Moreover, as per rules, the land
   owner shall get the map of approved project.

The land owner shall have the option of retaining part of 16 percent developed land
handed over to him and the owner shall obtain cash compensation for the remaining land
on the basis of mutual agreement. The acquiring body shall declare the rate of cash
compensation at the beginning of the project. Moreover, the land given to land owner
shall be free from development fee or land use conversion fee.

There are various benefits for each land owner, whose land has been acquired. Land
owner shall be given annuity of Rs.23,000 per acre per year in addition to compensation
amount. The amount of annuity shall be increased each year by Rs.800 per acre in the
month of July. Land owner, who does not want to take annuity, shall be given a lump sum
amount of Rs. 2,76,000 per acre as rehabilitation subsidy. In case the land is acquired for
a company, the land owner shall have option to obtain shares of the company equivalent
   129

to 25 percent amount of the lump sum subsidy. During the implementation of the project,
each family which becomes landless, shall be given 40 sq m developed residential land
free of cost. A financial help equivalent to the minimum agricultural wages for 5 years as
compensation for livelihoods shall be given to each affected family whose total land has
been acquired. Moreover, financial help equal to minimum agriculture wages equivalent
to 500 days as compensation for livelihood loss is given to the family whose total land has
not been acquired and has become marginal farmers due to implementation of the
project. In order to support small farmers, each family affected by acquisition of land shall
be given financial help equivalent to minimum agricultural wages for 375 days. One-time
financial help provided equal to minimum agricultural wages of 625 days shall be given
to each affected family of agricultural or non-agricultural laborers. Each affected family
displaced by the project shall be given compensation for livelihood equal to minimum
agricultural wages of 250 days. In case of hereditary land, land owners shall continue to
get additional facilities according to prevailing practice.

A Kisan Bhawan would be constructed by the developer agency of the project at its own
cost in every village affected by land acquisition in order to compensate the land owners
so that they can have a building for their community requirements. Additionally, a
scheme of at least one model school up to class 8 with a playground would be started in
the project area and the building for it would be constructed by the developer of the
project at its cost for providing education opportunities to the children of the landless
laborers and land owners living below poverty line. The developed land given back to the
land owners as compensation shall be exempted from stamp duty and registration fee
payable on registration.

The compensation package shall be determined by mutual agreement between the land
owner and the developer at the village itself and the Collector of the District shall act as a
facilitator. In this case, instead of land being acquired shall be directly transferred by the
land owner to the developer of the project. The package shall be prepared only after
consent of at least 80 percent of the owners of the land is obtained.

Land of all those remaining farmers who do not agree to take the above package would
be acquired by adopting the process as provided under the Land Acquisition Act 1894. In
case, less than 80 percent of the total affected land owners give their consent, then the
project would be reconsidered.

In the New Noida, the U.P. Government could opt for land pooling instead of land
acquisition, which would help both land owners and state government. As per the
provision of land pooling policy, apart from compensation amount provided to land
owners, they will also get 25 percent land, which they are free to develop or sell.

14.1.3 Land Acquisition Pattern Of The Dedicated Freight Corridor Project

On Eastern Corridor, Delhi Freight Corridor (DFC) passes through the states of West
Bengal, Bihar, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Punjab. The Western Corridor will
traverse the distance from Dadri in Uttar Pradesh to Jawaharlal Nehru Port (JNPT),
Mumbai, passing through the states of Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Rajasthan, Gujarat and
Maharashtra. For the DFC, linear pattern of land acquisition will be required for project
design.

   130

The alignment has been designed to avoid or minimize the demolition of permanent
structures, local communities, city planning areas, residential areas, swampy areas, and
quarry sites. The alignment runs parallel to the existing railway line by utilizing the
existing railway land as much as possible to minimize land acquisition, while it takes
detour to the existing railway line to avoid densely populated areas. However, some land
acquisition is still required in both parallel and detour sections.

14.1.4 Legislation and Policy for Land Acquisition and Rehabilitation and
   Resettlement for the DFC Project

Railways (Amendment) Act, 2008: Under the Railways (Amendment) Act, 2008, land
acquisition is being carried out for the DFC Project, which is declared as Special Railway
Project. Land Acquisition Act 1894 is not applied for land acquisition under this Act.

National Rehabilitation and Resettlement Policy, 2007: In case of DFC project, a
narrow stretch of land is to be acquired, para 7.19 of the National Rehabilitation and
Resettlement Policy, 2007 shall be used for linear land acquisition for railway projects
and is basically applicable to the DFC projects. Objective of Rehabilitation and
Resettlement Policy, 2007 are listed below:

 •   To avoid or minimize land acquisition and involuntary resettlement impacts by

 •   To ensure adequate and expeditious implementation and rehabilitation package of
   rehabilitation process with the active participation of affected families.

 •   To provide special care for weaker sections like SCs or STs or other vulnerable
   groups.

 •   To facilitate better standard of living and providing sustainable income to Project
   Affected Persons (PAPs).

 •   To enable harmonious relationship between the requiring body and affected

equivalent to sixty percent on such market-value, which will be paid in consideration of

year. In case of tenants and lease holders an apportionment of the compensation payable
to structure owners for registered lessees (by local laws) shall be done. Further 3 month
written notice + Rs. 10, 000 shifting allowance for tenants to be provided. In case 3-month
notice is not given, 3 months rental allowance shall be given.

holders are encroachers, a cash compensation for loss of structures to be given only if 3
months’ notice is not given. In case the title holder is a squatter, cash assistance for
structures at replacement cost is to be provided.

Department for crops, etc.). Moreover, three months advance notice is to be issued to
growers of harvest fruits, crops and trees.

the reconstruction of community structures and replacement of common property
resources shall be appropriately done.

4,000 per household is to be provided. Additionally, training assistance of Rs. 4,000 for
income generation per household is to be provided.

rehabilitation grant equivalent to 750 days of minimum agricultural wages to those
families losing livelihoods shall be provided.

financial assistance of Rs. 10,000 as shifting allowance. Moreover, each affected family

   132

that is displaced and has cattle shall get financial assistance of Rs.15,000 to construct
cattle sheds.

Traders and Self-employed: In this case each affected person who is a small trader,
rural artisan, or self-employed person and who has been displaced shall get a onetime
financial assistance of Rs.25,000 for the construction of working sheds or shops.

In case of project affected persons who are rendered landless or reduced to the status of
small or marginal farmers due to land acquisition, they shall be entitled to rehabilitation
grant equivalent to 750 days of minimum agricultural wages.

additional financial assistance equivalent to a minimum of 300 days of agricultural wages
for vulnerable persons shall be given if they are not provided with alternative livelihoods,
and who are not otherwise covered as a part of family.

Poverty Line: People living below poverty line are provided house construction
assistance equivalent to the latest construction costs under the Indira Awas Yojana
Scheme for Rural Areas and cost of house construction under the Jawaharlal Nehru
National Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM) for urban areas. Moreover, temporary
employment in project construction work to affected persons with particular attention to

installment and rest at the time of taking over the possession of land.

14.1.24   Up Bio Energy Policy, 2022

The UP-Bio Energy Policy 2022, launched in September 2022 by the Government of Uttar
Pradesh, represents a significant stride towards sustainable energy production by
fostering the establishment of Compressed Biogas (CBG) plants, biodiesel production
plants, and bio-coal production plants. This policy is designed to leverage bioenergy
waste, offering a comprehensive suite of financial incentives and logistical support to
lower the barriers to entry for investors and promote widespread adoption.

Key incentives include substantial financial support, such as Rs 75 lakh per tonne (up to
Rs 20 crore) for CBG plants, Rs 75,000 per tonne (up to Rs 20 crore) for bio-coal plants,
and Rs 3 lakh per tonne (up to Rs 20 crore) for biodiesel plants. Additionally, the policy
offers a state subsidy covering 30% of equipment costs, supplementing a 50% central
subsidy under the Agriculture Mechanization Scheme. Infrastructure subsidies are also
provided for constructing approach roads up to 5 km, with a maximum investment of Rs
50 crore. Further benefits include exemptions from development charges, 100% waivers
on stamp duty and electricity duty, and government land available at a nominal lease rate
of Rs 1 per acre per annum, along with deemed permissions under the Change in Land
Use and Land Ceiling Act.

These incentives are strategically designed to reduce the financial and operational
burdens on investors, making bioenergy projects more viable and attractive. By doing so,
the policy aims to stimulate economic growth, create jobs, enhance energy security, and
contribute to environmental conservation through sustainable waste management
practices. To ensure the success of this policy, it is recommended to conduct awareness
campaigns, streamline application processes, and implement robust monitoring and
evaluation frameworks. These measures will help maximize the policy's impact and
facilitate the efficient execution of bioenergy projects.

In conclusion, the UP-Bio Energy Policy 2022 positions Uttar Pradesh as a leader in
renewable energy, setting a strong precedent for other states. It aligns with the broader
objectives of the DNGIR 2041 Master Plan by promoting sustainable energy solutions,
driving economic development, and contributing to environmental sustainability. This
policy not only fosters a greener future but also enhances the state's role in the national
and global renewable energy landscape.
